newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU starts BSE legal action against 10 countries.
newsitem.headline: EU starts BSE legal action against 10 countries.

text.p: The European Commission on Thursday started legal action against 10 countries for allegedly failing to respect EU animal feed production rules aimed at stamping out mad cow disease, a Commission spokesman said.
It has written to France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, Sweden and Finland giving them formal notice and asking for their comments within a month.

EU veterinary inspectors found that these countries were not properly implementing rules requiring meat and bone meal to be processed at higher temperatures and for longer periods so as to kill the infectious agents of the disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease).
The 10 countries were also criticised for not enforcing a 1994 ban on feeding ground-up cattle, sheep and goat meat and bone meal to animals.

"Meticulous implementation of all legislation relating to BSE is vital if it is to be eradicated and the possible risks to human health...avoided," EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said in a statement.
Infected meat and bone meal mixed into cattle and sheep feed is believed to be the main cause of the BSE epidemic, which has killed more than 165,000 cattle, mostly British, over the past 10 years.

A British government admission in March 1996 that BSE could be transmitted to humans, who ate infected beef, in the form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob-Disease (CJD) triggered consumer panic across Europe and an EU ban on British beef exports.
France has refused to apply the new meat and bone processing rules, which came into force on April 1, contesting their efficiency and legality.
Germany and Spain have argued that the rules are unnecessary for processing material from healthy animals.
But the EU Commission says it is impossible to be completely certain that the animals are totally free of BSE-risk.
Other countries are criticised for not properly implementing the processing rules or enforcing controls.
Fischler said in the statement that he hoped member states would take corrective measures as soon as possible so that the legal proceedings could be dropped.
